docs.title: IMP -- Improved Manual Pages
docs.text:
IMP is an open-source project focused on providing the best manual pages with examples for developers to understand

We noticed a problem with almost all manual pages, Which is they rarely give examples, Some people may not understand what manual pages mean by something unless they see examples

That's why I created IMP

On the left side, You will see a navigation icon. Click on it. You will find all manual pages that I made

docs.title: errno error codes - codes that say what's wrong
Description
docs.text: errno error codes are short codes in most systems (specifically Linux systems) that define what is the error

docs.title: List of error codes
docs.text:
EPERM: You can't do this operation with the current permissions

ENOENT: There is no file or folder with that name

ESRCH: The process does not exist

EINTR: System call has been stopped

EIO: Problem in I/O (input and/or output)

ENXIO: The requested device or address is not avaliable

E2BIG: The argument list is too big

ENOEXEC: There is a format error in Exec

EBADF: The requested file descriptor is not correct or does not exist

ECHILD:

EAGAIN: The requested resource is not currently avaliable

ENOMEM: There is not enough memory to allocate what you want to allocate

EACCES: You don't have required permissions to be able to do this operation

The list will be continued later

docs.title: Library
docs.text: Standard C library (libc)

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: fgets(char buffer, int size, FILE *stream)

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
fgets() is used to read user input from a stream (usually stdin, standard in)

Reading of text stops at an EOF (End-of-file) or a new-line character

The fgets() output returns as a char *

A null-terminator (\0) is stored after the last character from the buffer and indicates that the text has been finished

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: fgets() returns s on success and NULL on error or EOF (end-of-file) if there was an error, errno is set to say what's wrong

docs.title: Example without edge cases
docs.text:
#include <stdio.h>


char buffer[50];


int main() {
    printf("Enter a word: ");
    fgets(buffer, sizeof(buffer), stdin);   
    printf("\nThe word you entered is: %s", buffer);

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Example with edge cases
docs.text:
// You may want to add extra code if the program will perform other functions
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

char buffer[50];


int main() {
    printf("Enter a word: ");

    if (fgets(buffer, sizeof(buffer), stdin) == NULL) { // fgets() returns NULL on an error, s on success
        perror("fgets() error"); 
    }
    int length = strlen(buffer); // Count the characters of the user input for handeling edge cases, See strlen(1) for details

    if (strchr(buffer, '\n') == NULL) { // If fgets() didn't capture the newline character then more than 49 characters (not a fixed-number) has been inputed
        printf("You entered more than 49 characters, input will be truncated\n");
    }

    printf("\nThe word you entered is: %s", buffer);

    return 0;
}

docs.text: errno file on the website to know what errno is and provide a list of error codes and their meanings

docs.title: Description
docs.text: mkdir is a tool to make director(ies) if they do not already exist on Linux and other operating systems.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
-m, --mode=FILE_MODE specifies the file mode (permissions) for the directory that you are trying to create

-p, --parent no errors if the directory doesn't exist. Create parent director(ies) until we reach the target destination. This option is not affected by the -m option

-v, --verbose print extra information on directory creation

-Z sets SELinux security context to the default value defined by the system's policy

--context set the SELinux security context to the context specified in context=(SELinux security context) if blank, Set the default SELinux system security context for that file path

--help prints the help menu

--version prints the current version of mkdir

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
To create a directory, use this command without the "[]"

mkdir [directory_name]

docs.title: Library
docs.text: Standard C library (libc)

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text: mkdir(const char *path, mode_t perms);

docs.title: Description
docs.text: mkdir() makes a new directory specified in path with permissions perms (see inode(7))

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: mkdir() returns the number 0 on success and -1 on failure. On failure, errno is set to say what's the error

docs.title: Example with no edge cases
docs.text:
// Without edge cases

#include <stdio.h>
#include <sys/stat.h>

char *path = ""; // Don't forget to change this to the path you actually want
mode_t perms = S_IRWXU | S_IRGRP | S_IXGRP | S_IROTH | S_IXOTH; // read inode(7) man page

int main() {

    mkdir(path, perms);
    return 0;
}

docs.title: Example with edge cases
docs.text:
// With edge cases

#include <stdio.h>
#include <sys/stat.h>

char *path = ""; // Don't forget to change this to the path you actually want
mode_t perms = S_IRWXU | S_IRGRP | S_IXGRP | S_IROTH | S_IXOTH; // read inode(7) man page

int main() {

    if (mkdir(path, perms) == -1) {
        perror("mkdir() error"); // After this is printed on the screen perror() print errno to say the exact problem
    }

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Library
docs.text:
Standard C library (libc)

You have to import the library string.h to be able to use strstr() and other functions

docs.title: Synopsis
docs.text:
strstr(const char Where_to_search_from, const char What_to_search_for);

Where (Where_to_search_from) is the variable that contains the content that we would like to search for a specific substring

And (What_to_search_for) is the text that we want to search for

For simplification we are going to call (Where_to_search_from) searchfrom and (What_to_search_for) searchfor

docs.title: Description
docs.text: strstr() searches for the first occurrence of searchfor in searchfrom

docs.title: Return value
docs.text: If searchfor is not found in searchfrom anywhere, strstr() will return NULL (NULL in C is not a string)

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>

char *searchfor = "open_terminal=true";
char *searchfrom = "open_terminal=true"; // Always true for this example since you need to change these variables anyways
int open_terminal = 0;                  


int main() {

    if (strstr(searchfrom, searchfor)) {
        open_terminal = 1;  
        printf("%d", open_terminal);
    }

    return 0;
}
